Amur whitefish (Coregonus ussuriensis) inhabits the cold, well-oxygenated waters of the Amur River basin, where its life history is tightly coupled with thermal conditions. At a stable temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a setting typical of laboratory rearing protocols, the maximum lifespan has been documented at approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years], a longevity that is comparatively modest for a coregonid of its size. The species attains a maximum recorded total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], corresponding to an ultimate wet body mass of 2880 grams [Wwi = 2880 grams], as estimated from length-weight regressions derived from extensive field sampling. These asymptotic dimensions place C. ussuriensis among the larger members of its genus, though considerable variation is observed across its fragmented riverine distribution. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, emerging from demersal eggs with an average diameter of approximately 1.5 millimeters, carry a remarkably small wet weight at birth of just 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a value that reflects the minimal maternal investment per offspring typical of pelagic-broadcast spawning fishes.

Reproductive development in female Amur whitefish proceeds gradually, with sexual maturation occurring well before the attainment of maximum body size. Puberty, defined by the onset of vitellogenesis and gonadal recrudescence, coincides with a total length of 28 centimeters [Lp = 28 centimeters], a threshold at which corresponding wet weight at puberty reaches 242 grams [Wwp = 242 grams]. These values were derived from long-term mark-recapture studies and otolith-based growth reconstructions spanning multiple cohorts within the middle Amur River. The relatively late maturation schedule, representing nearly half the ultimate length, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth and energy reserve accumulation prior to reproductive investment. This pattern is consistent with that observed in other cold-water coregonines inhabiting resource-limited environments, where delayed maturity enhances fecundity and offspring survival during the first reproductive event. Females at the pubertal length are capable of spawning, though their clutch sizes remain substantially smaller than those of fully grown adults.

Under the same thermal regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C] that defines optimal growth conditions in captivity, a fully mature female produces approximately 33300 eggs per year, distributed across multiple spawning events. Individual spawning events yield approximately 1000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 1000 eggs per clutch], and a female can produce approximately 33 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 33 clutches per year]. This reproductive tactic, common among iteroparous salmonids, allows a single large female to deposit tens of thousands of eggs over a single breeding season, with individual clutch sizes ranging from several hundred to over a thousand eggs per spawning bout. The sustained output is energetically demanding and is supported by intensive feeding during the pre-spawning period, during which adult fish accumulate substantial lipid reserves in their musculature and visceral fat bodies.

The ecological context of this reproductive strategy becomes clearer when examining growth trajectories from hatchling to adult. A female at puberty weighing 242 grams [Wwp = 242 grams] has already undergone a mass increase of more than five orders of magnitude relative to its birth mass of 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], an extraordinary growth trajectory driven by the rich zooplankton and macroinvertebrate resources of the Amur River floodplain. The total length of 28 centimeters [Lp = 28 centimeters] at this transition point is a reliable field marker for fishery managers assessing the reproductive status of wild populations. Continued growth beyond puberty, ultimately reaching 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters] and 2880 grams [Wwi = 2880 grams], is supported by a shift toward piscivory in larger individuals, who feed extensively on small cyprinids and juvenile lampreys. This ontogenetic dietary shift allows older fish to sustain both tissue upkeep and the high metabolic costs of annual reproduction across a lifespan of 14 years [am = 14 years] at 17 °C [T = 17 °C].

Comparative analyses with congeneric species highlight several distinctive features of Coregonus ussuriensis life history. The ultimate length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters] is intermediate between the smaller C. peled and the much larger C. nasus, while the age at puberty defined by a length of 28 centimeters [Lp = 28 centimeters] and a mass of 242 grams [Wwp = 242 grams] suggests a relatively early maturation for a fish of its asymptotic size. This pattern likely reflects the selective pressures of a riverine environment with pronounced seasonal flooding, where opportunities for successful spawning and larval drift are temporally constrained. The birth mass of 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams] places the species near the lower end of the coregonid range, consistent with its production of small, pelagic eggs that are dispersed over vast distances during spring floods. Field surveys conducted at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] have confirmed that maximum longevity does not exceed 14 years [am = 14 years], a value that aligns well with predictions based on body size and metabolic scaling within the subfamily Coregoninae.
